sections.learningObjectives:
- Collect and verify patient demographic information accurately during new-patient registration.
- Explain the purpose and steps of new-patient registration in an ambulatory care setting.
- Identify and update demographic, contact, and insurance information correctly when patient details change.
- Verify patient identity using at least two identifiers to prevent wrong-patient errors.
- Apply privacy safeguards to protect protected health information at the front desk.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Demographics are the "about you" section on a form: your name, your birthday, where you live, and how to reach you.

### Question 2

If your name or address is typed wrong, the office might send your bill to the wrong house or mix you up with someone else — accuracy keeps everyone safe.

### Question 3

Your birthday is a basic fact about who you are, like your name — that is why it belongs on the registration form.

### Question 4

The registration form is like the first page of a new folder for a patient — it sets up everything the office needs to know about them.

### Question 5

Using two facts about you — like your name and birthday — is like using two keys instead of one to open the right locker.

### Question 6

Just like you re-check a name on a label every time, the office re-checks who you are each visit to make sure it has the right person.

### Question 7

The record uses your official name, the one on your ID, so all your papers match up — nicknames can go in a separate note.

### Question 8

We write your real name in the official box and put the name you like to be called in a special note, so both are respected.

### Question 9

The card is like an official name tag, so we copy it exactly and add a little note that you like to be called Jon.

### Question 10

Writing the birthday the same exact way every time is like always writing the date on homework the same way — so nothing gets mixed up.

### Question 11

If two papers show different birthdays, you would check which one is right before crossing anything out — the assistant does the same thing.

### Question 12

If you are not sure how to spell a friend's name, you ask them to spell it — the assistant does the same with patients.

### Question 13

Reading back is like checking your answer out loud so someone can catch a typo before it is permanent.

### Question 14

An emergency contact is the person the office calls if they cannot reach you — like the number you give a school for your parent.

### Question 15

The guarantor is the person who is responsible for the bill — like the grown-up who signs to pay when you go somewhere.

### Question 16

Finding out the language you speak best helps the office talk with you clearly, like choosing subtitles in your own language.

### Question 17

We keep your official name on the paperwork but write down how you like to be called, so everyone gets it right.

### Question 18

A new patient is someone who has never been here before, so we build their file from scratch; a returning patient just updates the file we already have.

### Question 19

When you move, the office has to change your address in the file, or your mail will keep going to the old house.

### Question 20

If you get a new phone number, the office updates it right away so they can still reach you — like updating your number in a school directory.

### Question 21

When you get a new card, the office copies it right away so the right insurance gets billed — like updating your payment info at a store.

### Question 22

Just like you re-check a phone list before a party, the office re-checks your details at each visit to keep everything current.

### Question 23

If your last name changes, the office updates it everywhere in your file, like correcting your name on a class roster.

### Question 24

If you find two folders for the same person, you fix the mix-up carefully before adding anything new — not make a third folder.

### Question 25

If two kids in class have the same name, you use their birthdays to tell them apart — the office does the same thing.

### Question 26

Showing your photo ID is like showing your library card — it proves you are who you say you are.

### Question 27

Copying both sides of the card is like copying both sides of a flashcard — you need all the information, not just half.

### Question 28

If two of your cards show different names, the office asks which is your correct official name before writing it down.

### Question 29

For a child's file, the office needs the grown-up in charge — like a parent — to be the responsible person on the account.

### Question 30

If someone cannot speak for themselves, the office asks the person who is legally in charge of them — like a parent — to help fill in the form.

### Question 31

The front desk is like a private conversation spot — what patients say about themselves should stay between them and the office.

### Question 32

If a sign-in sheet shows everyone's name and why they are sick, other people in the room can read private things — so the sheet should ask for less.

### Question 33

If someone starts talking about private things too loudly, you move to a quieter spot so others cannot hear.

### Question 34

A computer screen with patient info is like an open notebook of secrets — you turn it so other people cannot read over your shoulder.

### Question 35

You would not leave a note with someone's private information out where everyone can read it — you would flip it over or put it away.

### Question 36

Before telling someone anything about a patient, the office first checks that they are allowed to know — like checking ID before giving out a package.

### Question 37

Even if it is family asking, the office cannot share your private health details unless you say it is okay first.

### Question 38

What one patient tells the office is a secret, so the office will not talk about other patients — even to a friendly neighbor.

### Question 39

The office asks a couple of secret-ish facts about you, like your birthday, before telling you anything private over the phone.

### Question 40

When leaving a message, you say just enough — "please call us back" — instead of leaving all the private details on the machine.

### Question 41

Before sending private information, you double-check the address or number, just like checking the address before mailing a secret letter.

### Question 42

Papers with private information are shredded, like tearing up a secret note so no one can read it later.

### Question 43

You only take out the tools you need for the job — the office only uses the pieces of your information that are actually needed.

### Question 44

If you mail a secret to the wrong house, you tell a grown-up in charge right away so it can be fixed — the assistant tells the supervisor.

### Question 45

The office calls you quietly by your first name instead of shouting your full name and health details to the whole room.

### Question 46

A little wall or space at the desk is like a quiet corner that keeps private talk from being overheard.

### Question 47

If a friend starts sharing private news too loudly, you quietly suggest moving somewhere more private.

### Question 48

If someone is too close during a private talk, you politely ask them to wait a step back so the conversation stays private.

### Question 49

PHI is private health stuff with your name attached to it — like your name next to what the doctor found.

### Question 50

Only the people who need your information to do their job get to see it — like only the teacher who grades your paper reads it.

### Question 51

Typing two numbers in the wrong order is like dialing a phone number backwards — you reach the wrong person.

### Question 52

Writing dates the same way every time is like always putting the same number first, so nobody mixes up the month and day.

### Question 53

Writing things out fully is like using your whole name instead of a scribble, so no one misreads it later.

### Question 54

If you do not want to fill in one box on a form, the office should be okay with that and just leave it blank, not make up an answer.

### Question 55

If a card has an old date, the office asks you to check whether it is still good, like checking an expired coupon before you use it.

### Question 56

If what you wrote earlier and what you say now do not match, the office asks which is right and fixes it so mail goes to the right place.

### Question 57

A PO box is where you get mail, but the office may also need to know where you actually live — two different pieces of information.

### Question 58

Before putting a form in the file, you make sure every important box is filled in and easy to read, like checking homework before turning it in.

### Question 59

Your information is kept safely in the office's computer file, like keeping important papers in a locked folder.

### Question 60

The assistant is the careful note-taker who writes down all the important details, not the doctor who decides the medicine.

### Question 61

The assistant can help check with the insurance company, but cannot promise what they will pay — like checking a menu without promising the meal is free.

### Question 62

Checking that an insurance card is still good is a paperwork job, like checking a card is still valid before using it.

### Question 63

Consent forms are like a permission slip — they show the patient said yes and understood the rules before care starts.

### Question 64

Before the office sends your private records, you have to sign a paper saying it is okay — like signing to release your report card.

### Question 65

Even if you say it out loud, the office still needs your signed permission paper before sending your private records to someone else.

### Question 66

If your emergency contact changes, the office writes down the new person's number right away, so they can reach the right person in an emergency.

### Question 67

Writing down both numbers is like saving two ways to reach a friend, so you have a backup.

### Question 68

The office writes down what was checked and when, like dating and signing your homework so everyone knows when it was done.

### Question 69

Saying hello is nice, but the assistant keeps your private details quiet so other people do not hear them.

### Question 70

Getting the paperwork right first is like setting the table before dinner — everything after goes more smoothly.

### Question 71

Even when forms are filled out online, someone still checks that everything is complete and signed, like proofreading an email before sending it.

### Question 72

A photo check is one more way to be sure it is really you, but the office still confirms your name and birthday too.

### Question 73

When your name changes, it is updated in every place your name appears, like changing it on all your school papers at once.

### Question 74

The office quickly asks if your details are still the same, like checking your phone number is still right before sending a message.

### Question 75

The people at the front desk learn the rules for keeping secrets safe, because they hear private things all day.

### Question 76

If someone cannot hear well, the office finds a quiet spot or writes things down, so the private details stay private.

### Question 77

When someone needs help with language, the office brings a trained helper and finds a private spot, so nothing is misunderstood or overheard.

### Question 78

Talking about someone's private business where others can hear is like telling a secret in a crowded room.

### Question 79

If a secret slips out, the right thing is to tell the person in charge right away so it can be handled properly.

### Question 80

The office asks you to say your birthday quietly, rather than reading it out loud where others can hear.

### Question 81

If something seems wrong, the assistant quietly tells the boss instead of yelling or guessing — like telling a teacher instead of starting a fight.

### Question 82

The office writes down the new address plus when it was changed, like dating a note so everyone knows when it was updated.

### Question 83

If nothing changed, the office just makes a note that you confirmed it is the same — no need to rewrite everything.

### Question 84

Before opening a new folder, the office checks whether you already have one, so there are not two folders for the same person.

### Question 85

The office writes everything down correctly AND keeps it a secret — both matter at the same time.
